transcript.text: hi, we keep losing customers every month and i dont know what to do about it

Losing customers month after month is worth taking seriously. Quick thing that will shape what I suggest: if you knew in advance which customers were about to leave, what could you actually do for them — a call, an offer, a check-in — or is it invisible until they're already gone?
we could maybe call some of them, but only about 300 a month

That capacity is a useful ceiling to design around. Do you have an export of your customers you could share — one row per customer, with something in it showing who left in recent months? If so, what fields does it hold (plan, dates, spend, support tickets, anything like that)?
yeah we have an export with customer number, start date, plan, bill amount, support calls and whether they left. i haven't sent it yet

Sounds like the shape of the fix: rank customers by how likely they are to leave, and spend the 300 calls on the top of that list. To do that I need the export itself — could you upload it here (CSV or Excel is fine)? Nothing sensitive about the columns, but if customer number is a real phone number or email, let me know and we'll keep it out of the model.
i haven't sent it yet. customer number is just account no, not phone or email. can upload csv if needed

Yes — please upload the CSV here and I'll take it from there. Account number as a plain ID is fine; it won't be used as a predictor. Once it lands I'll check how many left and how many rows you have, then propose the shortest path to that ranked call list.
ok i'll upload it. tell me if you get it

Not yet — I've checked and no file has arrived on my side. Drop the CSV into this chat and I'll confirm the moment it lands. One thing worth noting when you send it: if the export covers many months of customers, that's actually better than a single snapshot, since we'd have more "left" cases to learn from.
yeah i think it has a few months but not fully sure. i'll upload it soon

Nothing's arrived yet — I'll confirm as soon as the CSV shows up. Meanwhile, one thing that will shape the target: if we get this right, what does winning look like six months from now — fewer customers leaving, or the same leavers but the bigger bills saved?
fewer leaving is main thing. i'll send the csv once i find it

Goal noted: fewer customers leaving, with ~300 calls a month to aim at that. The three cards above are what I'd do with the export — the ranked list is the one that fits your aim most directly, and the second checks whether calling is worth the capacity before you commit to it. Any of them starts the moment the CSV lands. When you find it, check it also includes customers who *stayed* — a file of leavers only can't be modelled.

choices.title: Ranked call list (model)
choices.what: Once the CSV is in, train a model on past churn to score every current customer by how likely they are to leave, then output the top ~300 each month. You get: A monthly ranked list of who to call, with a check that the top 300 leave far more often than average. Trade-off: Needs enough leavers in the file to learn from; accuracy builds up month by month. Effort: Bigger build — upload, then one training run and a scoring step each month.

choices.title: Is calling even the right lever?

Effort: Light — a few queries on the upload, written up as a decision memo.

transcript.text: which plan has the highest lifetime spend? quick pls [shares customers.csv]

[DCLab drew a chart with its numbers table above this message]

Quick answer, with one caveat: your table has no lifetime-spend column, so I estimated it as monthly spend × tenure. - **premium**: 89.39 per month over 29.08 months, across 228 customers — the highest by far
- **plus**: 48.41 per month over 27.43 months, across 369 customers
- **basic**: 19.22 per month over 29.22 months, across 603 customers

Premium wins on price, not on loyalty — tenure is close across the three plans. Chart and numbers are shown above. Is this for pricing and packaging decisions, or for spotting which customers to protect?
For pricing/packaging. Premium is the plan to push.

Plus retains best; premium earns most. - Premium isn't a business-customer story: 176 of its 228 customers are consumer, close to the mix on other plans. - Premium also has the fewest support tickets (1.12 vs 1.18 basic, 1.21 plus) and similar tenure. Caveat worth naming: that lifetime figure is spend × months already on the books, so it describes today's premium customers — not what a pushed-upgrade customer would do.

The plan comparison is done and shown above — nothing else is queued. If you want to go further from here, three natural next steps:

1. **Sizing the upside**: count how many basic/plus customers look premium-ready and what the revenue gap would be (quick, in this chat). 2. **A churn model** on `churned_next_month`, so pushes target customers likely to stick (a build with a holdout and metrics). 3. **A live dashboard** of spend, tenure, churn and tickets by plan. Which of those fits the pricing meeting — or shall I just take option 1?

(I left out the parts whose numbers I cannot source from you or your data. Ask me about any part in words and I will go through it.)
1. Quick sizing only, I need it today.

Quick sizing, first cut — the headroom isn't where the push points. Basic's single highest spender (37.87 a month) is still below the plus median of 48.45, so no basic customer is anywhere near premium pricing at 89.28. The upgrade pool sits in plus, your best-retaining plan at 11.1% churn (premium 14.5%, basic 22.4%) — each plus customer moved to premium adds the gap between those two plan prices, every month they stay. I'm counting only plus customers already at or above 48.45 who did not churn next month, as the safe push pool. Should I size it at today's premium median of 89.28, or a price you have in mind for the new packaging?
At 89.28. Size monthly and annual upside only.

[DCLab drew a chart with its numbers table above this message]

Sized at 89.28, chart and numbers above. - **Pool**: 158 plus customers at or above 48.45 who did not churn next month — together they spend 8,445.32 a month now, average 53.45. - **Monthly upside**: each one adds the gap between 89.28 and what they pay today, every month they stay. - **Annual upside**: twelve months of those same gaps, if all of them remain on the books for a full year. No basic customer qualifies — that plan tops out below the 48.45 line. One caveat for the meeting: in that plus price band, some customers churned the very next month, so the annual figure is a ceiling, not a forecast.

transcript.text: quick q: churn with 3% positives, should i report PR-AUC or ROC-AUC to my manager, and why? no data work, just the answer

Report **PR-AUC**, with ROC-AUC as a footnote. Why: with only 3% positives, ROC-AUC is flattered by the huge number of easy negatives — a model can look strong on it while catching almost no real churners. PR-AUC scores precision and recall on the rare class, so it moves only when your model actually finds churners. For your manager, pair it with one plain number: what share of churners you catch, and how many false alarms that costs. That's the decision they care about; a single AUC number, whichever one, doesn't tell them that.
